content.title: About
content.content: Parmesan, dry grated, fat free is a finely grated Parmesan cheese from which almost all fat has been removed. It retains the characteristic nutty aroma and intense flavor while providing a very low fat content, making it a convenient ingredient for diet‑friendly dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Parmesan is one of the oldest cheeses in the world; its production began in Italy over 800 years ago.
Grated Parmesan is often called “Parmesan flakes” and is used as a universal seasoning in many cuisines.
Fat‑free dry Parmesan contains a higher protein level per 100 g compared with regular grated Parmesan.
Traditional Parmesan is aged a minimum of 12 months, sometimes up to 36 months, which deepens its flavor.
In Italy, Parmesan holds a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status, guaranteeing its origin and production methods.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Fat‑free dry Parmesan provides about 35 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High calcium source
items.content: It contains over 1100 mg of calcium per 100 g, important for bone and dental health.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The reduced fat makes it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Parmesan supplies vitamins B2, B12 and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains probiotic bacteria
items.content: Grated cheese retains some live bacteria that may positively influence gut microbiota.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although lactose levels are low, individuals with severe intolerance may still experience symptoms.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Fat‑free dry Parmesan contains about 1500 mg of sodium per 100 g, which can be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein should avoid this cheese.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: Because of its nutrient density, it’s easy to exceed daily calorie goals if portions are not monitored.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sprinkle the cheese over pasta, salads, soups, and casseroles. It works well in sauces, omelets, or as a coating for fish and chicken. Its low fat content helps it retain shape during baking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cheese in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage, refrigerate or freeze it. Discard if you notice mold, off‑smell, or color changes.

fruit-and-vegetable-smoothie-with-dairy.title: Fruit and vegetable smoothie with dairy

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit and vegetable smoothie with dairy is a drink made from fresh fruits, vegetables and dairy ingredients (milk, yogurt, kefir). It combines the natural sweetness of fruit, the nutrients of vegetables and the probiotics of dairy, providing a light and tasty way to obtain vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Smoothies became popular in the 1970s in the United States as part of the health‑food movement.
Adding dairy improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E and K from fruits and vegetables.
Smoothies can be made with any combination of fruits and vegetables, allowing endless flavor and nutrition variations.
When stored properly, a smoothie retains most of its vitamins for 24–48 hours.
In many countries smoothies are commonly served in health‑food cafés and fitness centers.

items.title: Rich in vitamins C and A
items.content: Fruits and vegetables in the smoothie provide abundant vitamin C and beta‑carotene, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fermented dairy supplies probiotics that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of calcium and protein
items.content: Milk and yogurt deliver calcium and complete protein, essential for bones and muscles.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Phytonutrients from berries and leafy greens act as antioxidants, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high water content of a smoothie helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance should use lactose‑free or plant‑based milk alternatives.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Very sweet fruits can raise the drink’s glycemic index; balancing with vegetables is recommended.

items.title: Allergy to individual ingredients
items.content: Allergies to berries, nuts or dairy require omission of the offending component.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Citrus fruits may irritate a sensitive stomach; those with acid reflux should choose milder options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the smoothie cold in a glass or bottle. It works well as a breakfast, a post‑workout snack, or a refreshing drink any time of day. For extra texture and flavor, add chia seeds, nuts or a drizzle of honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared smoothie in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, freeze individual portions and thaw them in the fridge before drinking.

content.title: About
content.content: Pomelo (Citrus maxima) is the largest citrus fruit, native to Southeast Asia. It has a very thick yellow-green rind, firm segments covered in a bitter membrane, and juicy flesh from pale yellow to pink. The flavor is sweet with a light tartness, milder than grapefruit. Pomelo is eaten fresh and added to salads and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pomelo is the largest of the citrus fruits: a fruit can weigh more than a kilogram.
Grapefruit is a hybrid of pomelo and orange.
Before eating, the thick rind and the bitter membrane on the segments must be removed.
In China and other Asian countries, pomelos are given at Lunar New Year and the Mid-Autumn Festival as a symbol of prosperity.
The rind of pomelo is made into candied peel and added to tea.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Pomelo is low in calories and high in water.

items.title: Contains flavonoids
items.content: Citrus flavonoids have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Pomelo, like grapefruit, can affect how some medications work, such as statins and blood pressure drugs; if you take medications, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Pomelo is acidic and may cause heartburn or irritate tooth enamel.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: People with kidney disease who need to limit potassium should consult a doctor.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Citrus fruits can cause allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut off the top, score the thick rind on the sides and peel it, separate the fruit into segments, and remove the bitter membrane, leaving only the flesh. Eat the flesh fresh, or add it to salads, yogurt, desserts, and juices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A whole pomelo can be stored at room temperature for one to two weeks or longer in the refrigerator. Keep peeled segments in the refrigerator in a covered container for three to four days.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned tomato soup is a ready‑to‑eat product made from ripe tomatoes, water, salt and spices. It is served hot and often used as a quick meal or as a base for more elaborate dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato soup is among the most popular canned foods worldwide.
Lycopene content is retained during canning, making the soup a good source of antioxidants.
Tomatoes used for the soup are frequently grown in greenhouses, ensuring a consistent flavor year‑round.
Canning allows the product to be stored for 2‑3 years without loss of taste.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts the immune system and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: Tomato soup is low in calories, making it suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports muscle function.

items.title: Easy to prepare
items.content: Simply heat the soup in a microwave or on the stove for 5‑7 minutes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned soup can be high in salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or added spices.

items.title: BPA in packaging
items.content: Metal cans may contain traces of BPA; choose products labeled BPA‑free when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the soup until boiling, optionally add cream, herbs or croutons. It can also serve as a base for stews, pasta sauces, or risotto.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and consume within 3‑4 days, refrigerated.

taco-meat-with-beans-no-cheese.title: Taco with meat and beans, no cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A taco is a traditional Mexican dish consisting of a soft or crispy tortilla filled with meat, beans, and various seasonings. This version uses lean beef, cooked red beans, fresh vegetables, and spices, without any cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tacos originated in Mexico in the early 19th century as street food for laborers.
Traditionally the meat is grilled over an open flame, giving it a smoky flavor.
Beans in tacos provide a great source of plant protein and fiber.
Leaving out cheese makes the dish lighter and suitable for people with lactose intolerance.
Classic tacos are often served with lime, cilantro, and salsa.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef and beans together supply a complete set of amino acids, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Fiber from beans
items.content: Beans are high in soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting digestive health.

items.title: Low in lactose
items.content: The absence of cheese makes the dish safe for those with lactose intolerance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and beans provide B12, niacin, and riboflavin, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Using fatty cuts of beef can increase saturated fat levels, which may be a concern for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt and sauces can raise sodium intake, which should be limited for hypertension.

items.title: Bean allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to beans and should avoid this ingredient.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The combination of meat, beans, and tortilla makes the dish relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the tortilla, then fill it with beef, beans, fresh veggies (tomatoes, onion, lettuce) and seasonings. Optional toppings include salsa, guacamole, or a squeeze of lime.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared tacos are best eaten immediately. If needed, store meat and beans separately in airtight containers in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Tortillas can be kept at room temperature in a sealed bag for up to 5 days.
